title: 36-year tech veteran unpacks his strategy to crush the market in 2026
excerpt: Paul Wick has helmed the Columbia Seligman Technology and Innovation Fund for nearly four decades, delivering huge returns.

How a 36-year tech veteran is navigating AI worries and crushing the market this year

By William Edwards

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-03T10:00:01.212Z

Read in app

Investor of the Month spotlights professional investors who are outperforming their peers. It's less about crowning "the best" and more about digging into the portfolios, strategies, and decisions of traders taking unique steps to win right now.

Paul Wick had just two weeks to learn what it means to be a tech investor before he was handed the reins of the Columbia Seligman Technology and Information Fund (CCIZX) in 1990.

His predecessor was retiring and the firm needed a replacement, so the president moved him over from the high-yield bond strategy.

"It was a trial by immersion," Wick told Business Insider in an interview.

Thirty-six years later, Wick's performance speaks for itself. In the last decade-and-a-half, he's beaten 93% of US technology funds, according to Morningstar data. If you had invested $10,000 in the fund 10 years ago, it'd now be worth about $109,000.

Even during the AI-fueled market boom, Wick has continued to outperform. Over the last five years, he's outclassed 94% of his peers.

In 2026, the fund is handily beating the market again, even more remarkable given the volatility that has weighed on the AI trade and rattled the tech-led bull market. His fund is up almost 55% this year, compared to the 13% gain in the S&P 500.

The excitement of the job still gets him out of bed every morning.

"I like finding new ideas," he said. "The investment industry, especially technology, is changing so continuously that you are just forced to learn all the time."

Wick's investing secret sauce

So, what's underneath the hood at Columbia Seligman that sets Wick and his team apart?

Wick attributes his success to multiple factors. One of them is continuity at the fund. Not only has he been at the helm of the fund for 36 years, but most of his team have also worked with him for more than 10 years.

Another is the access he's given to companies the fund invests in. Part of that is because he's based in Menlo Park, California, in the heart of Silicon Valley. But it's also because of how large the fund and the firm have grown. CCIZX now oversees $29 billion in assets, while Columbia Threadneedle manages over $700 billion in assets.

"We're one of the largest investors in the US technology industry," Wick said. "Company managements want to see us. We get preferential access, I'd say, relative to a lot of other people. We're one of the first people management wants to call back after an earnings print to answer our questions."

There's also expertise. For example, Wick has two semiconductor analysts on his team who used to work in the industry.

And then there's strategy and stock selection. To identify companies, Wick and his team look for a few characteristics. They include:

  • Competitive moats: Does a company have a strong advantage over competitors and a product so good that customers are committed to paying up for it?
  • Caliber of management: Can the management team be trusted to deliver growth?
  • Valuation: Is the stock cheap? "Ideally, you want to find a great company that's been neglected by the market," Wick said.

CCIZX has had a heavy tilt toward the AI trade in recent years, Wick said, particularly capex beneficiaries.

After a big run-up in June, however, he said he trimmed several of his positions in that space, and has diversified into stocks in the software, internet, and cybersecurity spaces.

But now, with capex beneficiaries having been pretty beaten up over the last few months, he's finding good entry points in certain stocks.

He highlighted a few, including Lam Research, which produces machinery for making semiconductors, and Bloom Energy, which provides energy solutions for data centers. Lam is down 20% in a month, while Bloom Energy has fallen 22%.

Others include semiconductor producers like Onsemi and NXP, which trade at cheap valuations and have substantial revenue exposure outside of the AI trade, making them more defensive options if the AI trade goes awry.

Here are the fund's top 10 holdings and their weightings as of September 30:

  • Bloom Energy (9.48%)
  • Lam Research (5.38%)
  • Nvidia (4.79%)
  • Broadcom (4.78%)
  • Marvell Technology (3.41%)
  • Alphabet (3.3%)
  • Microsoft (3.02%)
  • Apple (2.92%)
  • GoDaddy (2.68%)
  • Western Digital (2.32%)

Deep dive: Who is Paul Wick?

Wick's responses have been edited for clarity and length.

Any favorite hobbies?

I like to play golf, tennis, scuba dive, and ski.

You can go to some pretty cool places to scuba dive. Where have you been?

I've gone all over the world, from the murky waters of New Jersey and Long Island and quarries in Pennsylvania, to the Red Sea, the Galapagos, all over the Caribbean, Thailand, Bali, Fiji, French Polynesia.

Diving in the Bahamas is definitely on my agenda for early next year.

You've got a wine cellar. Any favorite bottles you can remember?

We just had a 25th anniversary party for our hedge fund in California a little over a month ago, and I pulled out a bottle of Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cask 23 from 1994, and it was a 15-liter bottle of wine. It was phenomenal, phenomenal wine.

I knew the founder of Stag's Leap Wine Cellars, Warren Winiarksi, and I actually went to France with him to Bordeaux and Paris 19 years ago.

Favorite vacation spot?

We have a vacation home in Kona on the Big Island in Hawaii, and that's probably my favorite place to be.

One of your top career memories?

In our hedge fund strategy, we had been short a biotech company called Allakos. And with one week left in the year, both of the company's trials failed, and the stock was down 90% in one day. That was kind of a Christmas present.

How a 36-year tech veteran is navigating AI worries and crushing the market this year

作者：William Edwards 您目前正在关注该作者！ Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-03T10:00:01.212Z

Read in app

Investor of the Month spotlights professional investors who are outperforming their peers. It's less about crowning "the best" and more about digging into the portfolios, strategies, and decisions of traders taking unique steps to win right now.

Paul Wick had just two weeks to learn what it means to be a tech investor before he was handed the reins of the Columbia Seligman Technology and Information Fund (CCIZX) in 1990.

His predecessor was retiring and the firm needed a replacement, so the president moved him over from the high-yield bond strategy.

"It was a trial by immersion," Wick told Business Insider in an interview.

Thirty-six years later, Wick's performance speaks for itself. In the last decade-and-a-half, he's beaten 93% of US technology funds, according to Morningstar data. If you had invested $10,000 in the fund 10 years ago, it'd now be worth about $109,000.

Even during the AI-fueled market boom, Wick has continued to outperform. Over the last five years, he's outclassed 94% of his peers.

In 2026, the fund is handily beating the market again, even more remarkable given the volatility that has weighed on the AI trade and rattled the tech-led bull market. His fund is up almost 55% this year, compared to the 13% gain in the S&P 500.

The excitement of the job still gets him out of bed every morning.

"I like finding new ideas," he said. "The investment industry, especially technology, is changing so continuously that you are just forced to learn all the time."

Wick's investing secret sauce

So, what's underneath the hood at Columbia Seligman that sets Wick and his team apart?

Wick attributes his success to multiple factors. One of them is continuity at the fund. Not only has he been at the helm of the fund for 36 years, but most of his team have also worked with him for more than 10 years.

Another is the access he's given to companies the fund invests in. Part of that is because he's based in Menlo Park, California, in the heart of Silicon Valley. But it's also because of how large the fund and the firm have grown. CCIZX now oversees $29 billion in assets, while Columbia Threadneedle manages over $700 billion in assets.

"We're one of the largest investors in the US technology industry," Wick said. "Company managements want to see us. We get preferential access, I'd say, relative to a lot of other people. We're one of the first people management wants to call back after an earnings print to answer our questions."

There's also expertise. For example, Wick has two semiconductor analysts on his team who used to work in the industry.

And then there's strategy and stock selection. To identify companies, Wick and his team look for a few characteristics. They include:

  • Competitive moats: Does a company have a strong advantage over competitors and a product so good that customers are committed to paying up for it?
  • Caliber of management: Can the management team be trusted to deliver growth?
  • Valuation: Is the stock cheap? "Ideally, you want to find a great company that's been neglected by the market," Wick said.

CCIZX has had a heavy tilt toward the AI trade in recent years, Wick said, particularly capex beneficiaries.

After a big run-up in June, however, he said he trimmed several of his positions in that space, and has diversified into stocks in the software, internet, and cybersecurity spaces.

But now, with capex beneficiaries having been pretty beaten up over the last few months, he's finding good entry points in certain stocks.

He highlighted a few, including Lam Research, which produces machinery for making semiconductors, and Bloom Energy, which provides energy solutions for data centers. Lam is down 20% in a month, while Bloom Energy has fallen 22%.

Others include semiconductor producers like Onsemi and NXP, which trade at cheap valuations and have substantial revenue exposure outside of the AI trade, making them more defensive options if the AI trade goes awry.

Here are the fund's top 10 holdings and their weightings as of September 30:

  • Bloom Energy (9.48%)
  • Lam Research (5.38%)
  • Nvidia (4.79%)
  • Broadcom (4.78%)
  • Marvell Technology (3.41%)
  • Alphabet (3.3%)
  • Microsoft (3.02%)
  • Apple (2.92%)
  • GoDaddy (2.68%)
  • Western Digital (2.32%)

Deep dive: Who is Paul Wick?

Wick's responses have been edited for clarity and length.

Any favorite hobbies?

I like to play golf, tennis, scuba dive, and ski.

You can go to some pretty cool places to scuba dive. Where have you been?

I've gone all over the world, from the murky waters of New Jersey and Long Island and quarries in Pennsylvania, to the Red Sea, the Galapagos, all over the Caribbean, Thailand, Bali, Fiji, French Polynesia.

Diving in the Bahamas is definitely on my agenda for early next year.

You've got a wine cellar. Any favorite bottles you can remember?

We just had a 25th anniversary party for our hedge fund in California a little over a month ago, and I pulled out a bottle of Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cask 23 from 1994, and it was a 15-liter bottle of wine. It was phenomenal, phenomenal wine.

I knew the founder of Stag's Leap Wine Cellars, Warren Winiarksi, and I actually went to France with him to Bordeaux and Paris 19 years ago.

Favorite vacation spot?

We have a vacation home in Kona on the Big Island in Hawaii, and that's probably my favorite place to be.

One of your top career memories?

In our hedge fund strategy, we had been short a biotech company called Allakos. And with one week left in the year, both of the company's trials failed, and the stock was down 90% in one day. That was kind of a Christmas present.
